title: Receive These Roses
text:
Receive these Costa Rican

roses,


Myriam, with these

love verses


my verses will remind you

that the faces


of the roses

resemble yours


the roses

will remind you

that love

must be cut,


And that your face

will pass like

Greece and Rome


When there is

no more love

nor roses from Costa Rica


You will remember, Myriam,

this sad song
editorial_note: The translation keeps the roses as both gift and warning that beauty and love are cut and pass away.

title: Suddenly in the Night a Siren Sounds
text:
Suddenly in the night an alarm

siren sounds, long, long,

the mournful howl of the siren

of fire or of the white ambulance of death,

like the cry of the Cegua in the night,

coming closer and closer over the streets

and the houses and rising, rising, and falling

and growing, growing, falling and moving away

growing and falling.

It is not fire or death:

It is Somoza passing.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the siren's physical movement through the city before naming Somoza as the threat.

title: It Is Not That I Believe the People Raised This Statue for Me...
text:
It is not that I believe the people raised this statue for me

because I know better than you that I ordered it myself.

Nor that I intend to pass with it into posterity

because I know the people will tear it down one day.

Nor that I wanted to raise for myself while alive

the monument you will not raise for me when dead:

rather I raised this statue because I know you hate it.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the dictator's monologue as an admission that the statue exists because it is hated.

title: Somoza Unveils the Statue of Somoza in Somoza Stadium
text:
It is not that I believe the people raised this statue for me

        because I know better than you that I ordered it myself.

        Nor that I intend to pass with it into posterity

        because I know the people will tear it down one day.

        Nor that I wanted to raise for myself while alive

        the monument you will not raise for me when dead:

        rather I raised this statue because I know you hate it.
editorial_note: This version preserves the catalog title and indented layout while translating the same anti-Somoza monologue.

title: As at Night Sings
text:
As at night sings

the esquirina


to the esquirín

who is on another

branch


"esquirín,

if you want me to go, I will go

if you want me to go, I will go;"

and to her branch the esquirín

calls her:


Esquirina,

If you want to come,

come


If you want to come,

come,"


and when she

goes where he is


the esquirín goes

to another branch:


that is how I call

to you,


and you go away


That is how I call to you,


and you go away.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the bird-call structure and the repeated withdrawal after the beloved is called.
